Unbiased metabolomics and lipidomics were then performed to provide complementary upstream information to the proteomic data, while also integrating different levels of biological information. LipidMatch processed lipidomics data acquired from LC-MS/MS analysis of lipid extracts identified 1,128 and 236 lipids out of 3,830 and 501 detected features in positive and negative ionization mode, respectively. Analysis of data from metabolite extracts using LipidMatch identified additional 848 and 419 lipids out of 3,819 and 3,843 detected features in positive and negative ionisation mode, respectively. Metabolomics data files processed with MS-DIAL identified 2,022 and 1,655 molecules. When comparing PDGFAB treated IZ with control IZ, we saw no changes in differential expression. Similarly, for PDGF-AB treated RZ with control RZ, we saw only 5 metabolites that were differentially expressed (Supplementary Fig.
7
). In the control group, comparison of RZ with IZ, revealed significant metabolic changes in the IZ, with downregulation of ether lipids (plasmanyl- and plasmenyl-phospholipids), CoQ
10
and glutamine as well as upregulation of the phosphatidylcholine pool. We also saw upregulation of acylcarnitine levels in the RZ [Fig.
6F
]. In the PDGF-AB group, when we compared RZ with IZ [Fig.
6G
], treatment appeared to negate the changes that were observed in the control group. Notably, there was also a significant downregulation of triglycerides within the remote zone. Additionally, we found a two-fold increase in pantothenic acid, which serves as a precursor for coenzyme (CoA) synthesis.
Our multi-omics data suggest altered expression of components involved in fatty acid oxidation in controls, while PDGF-AB treatment leads to a potential shift towards more efficient myocardial energetics, particularly within the RZ. Moreover, there appeared to be upregulation of proteins involved in redox balance in the PDGF-AB IZ. Collectively, these alterations could contribute to improved global myocardial function as a result of PDGF-AB treatment.
Discussion
Our study shows that PDGF-AB alters the properties of the post-MI myocardium and leads to significant improvement in cardiac function out to 58 days, even when overall scar size is comparable. This positive impact results from increased functional maturation of microvasculature, changes to infarct scar characteristics including increased scar alignment with improved myocardial mechanics. These are coupled with beneficial global changes with improved electrical organisation and the expression of several biological components (proteins, metabolites and lipids) involved in redox balance, as well as myocardial energetics.
To the best of our knowledge, this study also adds unique perspectives to the current literature pertaining to post-MI changes. A significant strength of this study was the longitudinal functional assessment at different timepoints with robust cMRI analyses as well as coronary pressure wire assessment. We substantially go further than the only other published study performing longitudinal cMRI assessment in a porcine model by Stoeck et al.
8
, who utilized a left circumflex artery occlusion method. A major difference in our study is our use of more prognostically relevant LAD occlusion and deeper mechanistic endpoints including histological analysis of the coronary microvasculature within scar, thorough investigation of the electrical properties of the post-MI microstructure and multi-omic assessment of the post-MI myocardium. Furthermore, this is only the second study that provides metabolomic/lipidomic data from a post-MI porcine model although Correia et al.
9
used Gottingen minipigs out to 90 days post-MI and did not have a therapeutic group nor perform functional longitudinal cMRI analysis.
We showed a significant improvement in LVEF at D30 and D58 post-MI in PDGF-AB treated animals, using longitudinal cMRI,. This confirms our previous results where we showed an improvement at D28 post-MI
7
but here we are able to show ongoing improvement in cardiac function at a later timepoint. Furthermore, we show that GCS was improved in the PDGF-AB treated animals and appears to be the primary driver for improved myocardial mechanics. Myocardial strain assessment using cMRI is now a validated tool
10
,
11
. The left ventricle comprises three distinct myocardial layers: subepicardial obliquely aligned fibres, mid myocardial circumferentially aligned fibres (related to GCS) and subendocardial longitudinally aligned fibres (related to GLS). Of these layers, longitudinal fibres are more susceptible to injury from hypoxia
12
. It has been shown that circumferential function contributes almost twice as much as longitudinal function to LVEF
13
and has been demonstrated using cMRI
14
. Hung et al.
15
have previously shown that an increase in end systolic volume (ESV), although associated with preserved circumferential function early post-MI, leads to deterioration in LV structure and function long term, while GLS did not significantly change despite an improvement in ESV
16
. The preservation of ESV in the PDGF-AB treated animals as compared to controls suggests that treatment mitigates post-MI adverse remodelling. Therefore, PDGF-AB continues to positively impact myocardial mechanics and cardiac remodelling after MI up to D58.
Mural cells are essential for maintaining vascular integrity and their absence leads to increased vessel permeability and microvascular dysfunction
17
. These findings align with our observations, which revealed increased microvasculature maturity in the PDGF-AB treated animals and an associated reduction in CFR decline and increased IMR. Increased NG2
+
positivity within the PDGF-AB treated microvasculature could point towards these mural cells being pericytes, which are known to strongly influence microvascular function
18
. These results add to our previous work showing increased angiogenesis at 28 days post-MI after PDGF-AB treatment
7
. Chintalgattu et al.
19
have shown that loss of mural cells leads to decreased CFR while inhibition of PDGFR function induces mural cell depletion. PDGFR-β signalling is involved in vascular maturation and is critical for regulating the coating of infarct microvasculature with mural cells, leading to their stabilization and maturation
20
. PDGFR-α signalling is not involved directly in vascular maturation
20
, but has been shown to play a pivotal role in matrix remodelling after a MI
21
, as the newly laid matrix provides a structural framework for formation of new blood vessels
22
. PDGF-AB is known to activate both PDGFR-α and PDGFR-β. Lastly, our proteomics data revealed that PLOD3 was upregulated in the PDGF-AB treated IZ. PLOD3 is involved in the synthesis of collagen IV, which is a critical component of the basement membrane
23
. This could potentially contribute to the increased vascular maturity seen in the PDGF-AB treated animals with the re-establishment of an intact basement membrane post infarct
24
. Therefore, PDGF-AB treatment leads to a functionally mature microvasculature post-MI that would aid in myocardial recovery and improving function.
PDGF-AB reduced heterogeneity within the scar and viable myocardium as well as number of local abnormal ventricular activations (LAVAs), suggesting a greater modulation of electrical properties of the post-MI myocardium. The heterogeneous nature of myocyte clearance and collagen deposition, as observed to be exacerbated in the IZ of control animals in our study, results in islands of surviving myocardial cells within healed infarct scars. This leads to the formation of channels that have an entry site, a protected isthmus, and a breakthrough exit site that activates the ventricles and can sustain VT
25
These alterations facilitate the conditions required to initiate and maintain sustained re-entrant ventricular tachy-arrhythmias. Inhomogeneous scars and/or heterogeneous necrosis, provide an ideal substrate for VT.
PDGF-AB had a beneficial effect in reducing the incidence of abnormal ventricular electrograms, regardless of infarct size. After MI, structural remodelling contributes to increased electrophysiological heterogeneity seen as LAVAs manifesting during electro-anatomical mapping (EAM) as discontinuous electrical propagation through myocardial bundles separated by fibrous tissue
26
. Attenuation of myocardial fibre heterogeneity within the scar tissue and organized collagen fibre alignment may contribute to improved mechanoelectrical feedback within scar tissue, thus preserving coordinated excitation-contraction coupling
7
. Sites of entrance and exit in a VT circuit are always characterised by LAVAs with observed electrogram fractionation. This is clinically relevant as abolition of this electrical substrate is used to guide post MI VT ablation procedures and is considered a measure of procedural success
27
. We hypothesize that the cellular re-organisation associated with PDGF-AB treatment corrects some of the disorganised electrical conduction associated with architectural derangement in scar tissue. Although we previously showed that VT induction was significantly less in the PDGF-AB group
7
, this was at 28 days post MI and scar homogenisation would continue to change over time. Sudden cardiac death after MI remains a significant cause of morbidity and mortality and is predicated by re-entrant conducting circuits in and around scar tissue, leading to ventricular tachycardia (VT)
28
. Alteration in the electrical conduction post-MI by PDGF-AB may lead to a decrease in morbidity related to arrhythmia and could present an exciting area of future study.
cMRI based DTI has emerged as a useful tool for assessment of myocardial fibre structure and geometry with high spatial resolution. This is based on the assumption that water diffusion along the myocardial fibre is the greatest, and therefore the primary eigenvector of the diffusion tensor coincides with the local fibre orientation
29
. Li et al. have shown that there is good correlation between ex vivo DTI and 3D histology using a rat model
30
. The breakdown of cell membranes within the infarct scar leads to fewer diffusion restrictions, thereby causing an elevation in MD and reduction in FA values
8
, with confirmation in in-vivo
31
,
32
and ex-vivo
33
DTI studies. In our study, PDGF-AB treatment lead to realignment of helicity, restoration of FA and improvement in MD, reflective of myocyte organisation, a potential driver for the improved cardiac function we have seen at D58 post-MI.
Our multi-omic analyses demonstrate that PDGF-AB treatment alters abundance of proteins and metabolites involved in redox balance and immunomodulation. This is the first study showing that abundance of ether lipids is downregulated in porcine infarct scar post-MI. Importantly, we show that ether lipids are downregulated only to a lesser extent in infarcts from PDGF-AB-treated animals when compared to control counterparts, suggestive of a possible PDGF-AB-induced protective role of ether lipids following MI. The antioxidant activity of ether lipid species is proposed to stem from their ability to form enyl-ether linkages, which react readily with several oxidants (e.g. reactive oxygen species (ROS)), thereby acting as a sink for ROS species during periods of oxidative stress
34
. Additionally, ether lipids also act as reservoirs of mediators such as prostaglandins, leukotrienes and resolvins, which all play critical roles in immune regulation
35
. We have previously shown at day 11 post MI that PDGF-AB treatment reduces pro-inflammatory cytokines and increase pro-reparative M2 macrophage numbers
6
. Given the role of ether lipids in biological processes that are impacted deleteriously during MI such as redox imbalance, one can presume that downregulation of these lipids may contribute to myocardial injury during MI, albeit this would need to be validated experimentally. Several other lines of evidence highlight the potential contribution of PDGF-AB in maintaining redox balance. We also saw a significant decrease of CoQ
10
levels in the control infarcts with decreased CoQ
10
levels shown to correlate with reduced LV function, as it is a potent antioxidant and ATP sparing agent
36
. We also saw an increase in GSS within the PDGF-AB IZ and glutathione is known to be a potent antioxidant
37
.
PDGF-AB appears to also regulate the expression of metabolites involved in myocardial energetics. For example, in the control RZ, there was a significant increase of acylcarnitine levels which would be suggestive of impaired fatty acid oxidation and reflect similar findings by Correia et al.
9
. Accumulated acylcarnitines can lead to cellular stress and lipid peroxidation, which could worsen cardiac dysfunction
38
Acylcarnitines have also been shown to be increased in the plasma of HF patients
39
. In contrast, PDGF-AB animals had a downregulation of triglyceride levels, suggestive of improved insulin signalling post-MI
9
, and re-utilisation of liberated fatty acids for synthesis of phospholipids, leading to improved oxidative phosphorylation. We also saw an increase in pantothenic acid, which is a precursor for CoA, which itself has been shown to improve cardiac dysfunction
40
and plays a critical role in the TCA cycle while also serving as a potent antioxidant
41
,
42
. Proteomic pathways involved in oxidative phosphorylation also appeared to be upregulated in the PDGF-AB treated IZ, suggesting improved energy production and alleviation of heart failure
43
.
There are certain limitations of the present study. We had a small sample size of
n
= 5 per group but achieved adequate statistical power. There was heterogeneity in the PDGF-AB treated samples (likely due to sampling and non-uniform therapeutic effect) for the multi-omics analyses which precluded direct comparison with the control animals. Further work to elucidate mechanisms underpinning the actions of PDGF-AB would be valuable but are out of scope of the current study,. Nevertheless, the results provided valuable insights into the changes occurring within the post-MI myocardium at day 60. PDGF-AB was delivered in isolation in a clinically relevant porcine model. The natural set of future experiments would include comparison with current optimal medical therapy as well as in combination to assess for an additive synergistic response. This study was conducted in female animals only and biological differences cannot be ruled out. A model incorporating a more severe injury e.g. proximal occlusion of the LAD or permanent ligation may affect the therapeutic efficacy of PDGF-AB. However, this porcine ischaemia-reperfusion model has been extensively validated in pre-clinical porcine heart failure studies
44
. Swine hearts share many similarities with human hearts, both in their baseline state and after myocardial infarction
45
. This improves the translational capacity of new therapies in the development pipeline.
In conclusion, we show in a clinically relevant porcine model of MI the extended efficacy (to 60 days post-MI) and exciting potential utility of PDGF-AB as an effective therapeutic agent to repair the infarcted heart. Our multi-modality protocol also provides invaluable unified data for an extended longitudinal assessment of post-MI changes in a porcine model.
Methods
All experiments were approved by the Animal Ethics Committee of the Western Sydney Local Health District. The ARRIVE guidelines
33
were followed in conducting animal research. 25 female Landrace swine, individually housed, received standard care. Animals were sourced at approximately two months of age from the same local supplier and acclimatised to the housing facility for at least two weeks before commencing experimental procedures.
Myocardial infarction induction and pressure wire measurements
After a 12 h fasting period, animals were premedicated with intramuscular ketamine (10 mg/kg), methadone (0.3 mg/kg), and midazolam (0.3 mg/kg). All animals were intubated and mechanically ventilated (Anestar-S, Datascope) at 10 ml/kg tidal volume with supplemental oxygen to maintain an end-tidal CO
2
of 35 to 45 mmHg. General anaesthesia was induced with intravenous Propofol (2–5 mg/kg) and maintained with 2% inhaled isoflurane. Anaesthetic depth was clinically monitored by cessation of movement, eye position, loss of muscular tone, and absence of palpebral and pedal reflexes. All animals were instrumented with a peripheral 24-gauge intravenous catheter in an ear vein, surface electrocardiography electrodes, a right femoral artery (6Fr) vascular access sheath as well as left femoral artery (5Fr) access for invasive hemodynamic monitoring. All vascular access was obtained under ultrasound guidance. 5000 units of unfractionated heparin was given after vascular access was established followed by maintenance boluses to maintain an activated clotting time (ACT) between 250 and 350 s.
The left coronary artery was engaged percutaneously via the right femoral artery using a 6Fr Hockeystick guiding catheter (Medtronic). We then proceeded to Coronary Flow Reserve (CFR) and Index of Microcirculatory Resistance (IMR) measurements using a RadiAnalyzer (Abbott Vascular, Santa Clara, California). A pressure-temperature sensor guidewire (Abbott Vascular, Santa Clara, California) was used. Pressure wire was calibrated, equalised just outside the guide catheter and then the sensor is placed in the distal 2/3 of the left anterior descending (LAD) artery. Intracoronary GTN (50–100 mcg) was given. Catheter was flushed with saline to ensure stable temperature. 3 ml of room temperature normal saline was injected through the guide catheter. Transit time was measured by the RADI. We ensured the values were within 10–15% of each other otherwise they were re-measured. 3 injections were performed to get a resting mean transit time (T
mn
Rest). Subsequently, maximal hyperaemia was induced with adenosine (400 mcg/kg/min). Hyperemic meant transit time (T
mn
Hyp) was measured as described for T
mn
Rest. P
d
(pressure at wire sensor) was measured by the RADI in real time. The derivation of IMR is based on Ohm’s law (the potential difference across an ideal conductor is proportional to the current through the conductor) applied to the coronary microcirculation. IMR is defined as the mean distal coronary pressure (Pd) minus venous pressure divided by flow. Because venous pressure is generally negligible relative to distal coronary pressure, it is ignored. Because flow is inversely proportional to the mean transit time, IMR is therefore defined as Pd divided by the inverse of the mean transit time or as Pd multiplied by T
mn
Hyp.
A bolus of IV Amiodarone 150 mg was given as a slow bolus at this time. This was followed by a bolus of Lignocaine (1 mg/kg) and continued as an infusion. A 0.36 mm coronary guidewire (Asahi Sion Blue) was delivered into the LAD. Myocardial infarction was induced by inflation with a 2.5 mm angioplasty balloon (Boston Scientific) for 90 min distal to the first diagonal. The first diagonal was defined as the first major diagonal of at least 1 mm caliber and 30 mm from the ostium of the LAD. Cessation of flow distal to the occlusion was confirmed angiographically. Occurrence of ventricular arrhythmias during this period were managed with IV Metoprolol and biphasic cardioversion as needed. Hemodynamic changes were managed with IV Metaraminol to maintain a mean arterial pressure above 55 mmHg. Coronary angiography was performed after reperfusion to confirm vessel patency. Control MI animals proceeded to recovery whereas PDGF-AB assigned animals underwent a mini-pump insertion
46
. PDGF-AB protein (Peprotech cat no. 100-00AB, lot#021600) was delivered at a fixed infusion rate of 65 μg/kg for 7 days. Sham animals underwent all aspects of the procedure except balloon inflation in the LAD. Animals were recovered and survived out to 60 days.
2-ml ALZET (Durect) osmotic mini-pump insertion
A line was drawn between the tip of the manubrium and the angle of the right ramus of mandible, about 5–6 cm long. A 50/50 mix of bupivacaine and lignocaine was injected through the skin and into the deeper tissues along the length of this incision. An incision was made through the skin and subcutaneous tissue followed by blunt dissection through the underlying muscle in the direction of the muscle fibres. Haemostasis was strictly maintained. The right internal jugular vein was dissected from the sheath. A pocket was created, using blunt dissection, for the mini pump cranial to the vein to allow for it to sit flush with the vein. A 5-0 monofilament was used as a purse string to aid control of the vein (generally recommended for haemostasis and handling). A 16-gauge intravenous cannula was passed into the vein to enable passage of the minipump tubing. A basket suture was tied around the minipump with 3-0 non-absorbable monofilament and the minipump was attached to the tubing (5 mm overlap). The minipump was placed beside the vein and tied in place to the medial muscle sheath. Muscle layer was closed followed by closure of the subcutaneous later along the intradermal suture line. The skin was sutured and a dressing placed in peri-operative period to keep the wound clean during recovery
46
.
Cardiac Magnetic Resonance Imaging
All cMRI examinations were performed on a Siemens 3 T Prisma (Siemens Medical systems, Erlangen, Germany) utilising an 18–channel body array anteriorly together with posterior spine array coils and 4–lead electrocardiogram (ECG) gating. All sequences except perfusion and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) were performed with breath-holding technique in end-expiration with one signal average. Expanded information on the DTI sequence is available within the article by Nguyen et al.
47
.
Axial and coronal TrueFISP (true fast imaging with steady state free precession) and axial HASTE (half Fourier Acquired-Single Shot spin echo) sequences through the chest were acquired to plan preliminary 2-chamber, 4-chamber and short axis stack (SAX) single slice images. True 4-chamber and 2-chamber single slice TrueFISP cines were then acquired, followed by 16 contiguous 8 mm SAX cine slices, starting just below the apex and extending into the pulmonary artery, planned from the 2 and 4 chamber cine images in end-diastole. Following this, RVLA, right 4-chamber, LVLA, LVOT1, LVOT 2, RVOT1 and RVOT2 single slice TrueFISP cines were acquired with the following parameters: TR: R-R interval of individual animal, TE: 1.3 ms, FOV: 320 mm, slice thickness: 8 mm, in plane resolution: 1.4 mm × 1.4 mm, flip angle: 70 degrees, retrospective reconstruction with 25 calculated phases, scan time around 10 seconds.
T1 (pre-and post-gad) mapping sequences were acquired with the same geometry as the SAX cine. FOV and in-plane resolution were the same for both maps (360 mm, 1.9 mm × 1.9 mm). Other parameters for T1 maps were TR: 263.88 ms, TE: 1.01 ms, flip angle: 35 degrees.
Diffusion tensor imaging sequence was acquired under free-breathing conditions with a protocol consisting of a 2DRF zoomed diffusion prepared spin echo(4), FOV = 350 mm, matrix = 128 × 48, 5 slices, 8 mm slice thickness, TR = 500 ms, 1 b0 acquisition, 12 diffusion directions at b = 500 s/mm
2
, 8 averages.
Pre and post contrast Angiography acquisitions using a fast low-angle shot three-dimensional (FLASH-3D) technique were planned in an orthogonal coronal plane with the following parameters: TR: 3.4 ms, TE: 1.21 ms, FOV: 370 mm, slice thickness: 0.87 mm, in plane resolution: 0.9 mm × 0.9 mm with acquisition time of 28 seconds. The post contrast phase was performed immediately following the perfusion sequence.
First-pass perfusion imaging was performed using a single shot gradient echo acquisition in SAX plane. Four to six slices (depending on individual R-R interval) of 8 mm thickness with a 4 mm gap were planned through the left ventricle. Gadolinium contrast (Gadovist) at 0.2 mmol/kg was given via automatic injector at a flow rate of 3.0 ml/s through a 22-gauge cannula placed in an ear vein. Other parameters were TR: 124.58 ms, TE: 0.89 ms, flip angle: 10 degrees, in plane resolution: 1.9 mm × 1.9 mm, acquisition time of around 1 min.
Late Gadolinium Enhancement (LGE) images were acquired for tissue characterisation using a segmented inversion recovery fast gradient echo sequence in SAX, LVLA and 4-chamber planes. TI (time of inversion) scout was performed at 9 min post contrast to select appropriate inversion time (usually around 300 ms) for DE acquisitions which began at around 11 min post-injection. The SAX was run with 30 contiguous slices of 4 mm thickness, covering the entire heart with in-plane resolution of 1.5 mm × 1.5 mm whereas for the LVLA and 4-ch sequences, single 8 mm thick slices were acquired with in-plane resolution of 1.4 mm × 1.4 mm. Other DE parameters were TR: R-R interval of individual animal, TE: 1.65 ms, flip angle: 20 degrees.
Flow data for the aortic and pulmonary outflow tracts was acquired separately with a phase contrast technique by planning a single slice 1–2 cm above each valve. Velocity encoding (VENC) scouts were performed to select correct VENC value for each of the outflow sequences which were then acquired with the selected VENC and the following parameters: TR: 37.12 ms, TE: 2.47 ms, FOV: 340 mm, flip angle: 20 degrees, slice thickness: 6 mm, in-plane resolution: 1.8 mm × 1.8 mm with an acquisition time around 9 seconds.
Left ventricle volume analysis
Assessment of volumes was done according to Society for Cardiovascular Magnetic Resonance guidelines
48
. Manual endocardial and epicardial contouring was performed on the short axis stacks. Left ventricle (LV) end-diastolic image was chosen as frame 1. LV end-systolic image was chosen based on the smallest blood pool within the LV cavity. The volume calculation included LV outflow tract blood volume. Papillary muscles were excluded from mass calculations. Volume analysis was conducted offline using dedicated software (Medis Suite MR 3.2, Medis Medical Imaging, Schuttersveld 9, The Netherlands).
Strain analysis
Global longitudinal strain (GLS) values were averaged from three apical views (4-, 3- and 2-chamber)
49
. Short axis strain values for global circumferential strain (GCS) were averaged from three different slices identified at the basal (first slice with complete circular myocardium in absence of the left ventricular outflow tract), midventricular (level of both papillary muscles) and apical level (smallest LV cavity that maintained blood-pool throughout the entire cardiac cycle). Strain analysis was performed offline using dedicated software (Medis Suite MR 3.2, Medis Medical Imaging, Schuttersveld 9, The Netherlands).
LGE analysis
Infarct size was quantified using the short stack late gadolinium enhanced images
48
. Endocardial and epicardial borders were manually contoured from LV base to apex. A semi-automated algorithm for scar quantification was then applied with a 5 standard deviation threshold used as a cut off for hyperenhancement, delineating areas of late gadolinium enhancement from normal myocardium. Infarct percent was then calculated by dividing infarct size by end diastolic left ventricular mass, as measured on the cine short stack acquisitions during end-diastole. LGE analysis was conducted offline using dedicated software (Medis Suite MR 3.2, Medis Medical Imaging, Schuttersveld 9, The Netherlands).
Native T1 and Extracellular Volume (ECV) analysis
Pre and post contrast T1 maps were used to generate ECV maps. Average global T1 and ECV times were derived from slices contoured with endocardial and epicardial borders from LV base to apex. T1/ECV map analysis was performed offline using dedicated software (Medis Suite MR 3.2, Medis Medical Imaging, Schuttersveld 9, The Netherlands).
DTI analysis
DTI parameters consisting of mean diffusivity, fractional anisotropy, and helix angle transmurality were determined using custom software in Python
50
.
Electrophysiology study
All subjects underwent electrophysiological study. An 8.5 Fr Agilis steerable introducer (Abbott Medical) was inserted into the right femoral artery under ultrasound guidance through which an Advisor HD Grid (Abbott Medical) multi-electrode electrophysiological catheter was advanced retrograde to the left ventricle. A 6 Fr decapolar electrophysiological catheter was positioned into the coronary sinus via the right femoral vein. The Ensite Precision EAM system (Abbott Medical) was used to generate a substrate map delineating scar, border and remote zones using bipolar and unipolar voltage cutoffs of 0.5–1.5 mV and 3–8.3 mV respectively
51
.
Programmed ventricular stimulation (PVS) was performed at twice diastolic threshold at the right ventricular apex (single site) using a programmable stimulator. A drive train (S1) of 8 beats at 400 ms was followed by up to 4 extrastimuli. Stimuli were rectangular pulses of 2 ms duration at twice diastolic threshold with a 3 s delay between each drive train. The initial extrastimulus was delivered at a coupling interval of 300 ms and then decreased in 10 ms steps to ventricular refractoriness. If the earliest possible extrastimulus (e.g. S1S2) failed to induce VT, that extrastimulus was delivered 10 ms outside the ventricular effective refractory period and an additional extrastimulus was added (e.g. S2S3) at a coupling interval of 300 ms. The additional extrastimulus was decreased in 10 ms steps in the same manner. Additional extrastimuli were added in a similar manner (always starting with a coupling interval of 300 ms) until VT, ventricular fibrillation (VF), or ventricular flutter (<200 ms cycle length [CL]) was induced or refractoriness of the fourth extrastimulus (S5) was reached. There was no set lower limit for the shortest permissible extrastimulus coupling interval. Isoprenaline infusion was not used to facilitate VT induction.
Inducible VT was confirmed using a second protocol. The modified Michigan protocol uses exclusively four extra stimuli. At each drive train cycle length of 350 ms, programmed stimulation is initiated with coupling intervals of 290, 280, 270, and 260 ms for the first through fourth extrastimuli. The coupling intervals of the extra stimuli are shortened simultaneously in 10-ms steps until an extrastimuli is refractory or an arrhythmia is induced. A positive PVS was defined as sustained monomorphic VT CL ≥ 200 ms for >10 s. The inducible VT terminated spontaneously or required therapy in the form of anti-tachycardia pacing (ATP) or biphasic shock.
Local abnormal ventricular activations (LAVAs) are defined as sharp, high frequency ventricular potentials that are distinct from the far-field ventricular electrogram. LAVAs were measured as a percentage of total number of points used on the electro-anatomical map in sinus rhythm.
Histology
Animals were euthanized with 75–150 mg/kg of IV potassium chloride. The heart was washed in normal saline before being sectioned. Sectioning was performed from the apex to the base at 5 mm intervals. The first section was termed “Apex” and each subsequent section was termed “L1” onwards. “L2” and “L4” were immediately taken for snap freezing. The remaining sections were fixed in 10% neutral-buffered formalin. Fixation was performed for 48 h with formalin being changed at 24 h. Samples were subsequently switched to 70% ethanol, processed and paraffin embedded. Processing, embedding, and sectioning of blocks was performed at the Westmead Histology Core Facility at Westmead Institute for Medical Research.
The frozen sections were cut along the length of the LV wall and divided into epicardium, mid myocardium and endocardium. Samples were taken from the infarct zone, border zone and remote zone as well as the right ventricle.
Picrosirius red and fast green staining
Staining was performed on 4 µm sections taken from Apex and L1. Slides were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated with gradient ethanol (100%, 100%, 100%, 70%) then water. For picrosirius red with fast green staining, slides were placed in 0.1% Sirius red in picric acid with 0.1% fast green (#SIRIUSFAST500, POCD) for 4 hr and washed in running water. Slides were then dipped in 100% ethanol 5 times, fresh 100% ethanol 10 times, incubated in xylene 6 times for 1 min each and mounted in permanent mounting media (#FNNII065C, Froninecat) before cover-slipping.
Immunofluorescence
Immunofluorescence analyses were performed on 4 µm sections taken from Apex and L1. Paraffin embedded pig tissue sections were deparaffinized in xylene and rehydrated through a series of ethanol washes (100%, 95%, 70%, 50% ethanol) and water. Antigen retrieval was performed by incubating the sections in heated 10 mM sodium citrate buffer and then washed using PBS + 0.1% Tween-20. The sections were blocked using commercial blocking buffer for 1 h at room temperature and then incubated in primary antibodies (NG2 (mouse; Santa Cruz Biotechnology #sc-166251)) at 1:200, aSMA-FITC (Sigma Aldrich #F3777-0.2 ml) at 1:400 and CD31 (rabbit; Abcam/Cat No. ab28364) at 1:50 overnight at 4 °C. The following day, the sections were washed and stained with secondary antibodies (anti-mouse 594 (ThermoFisher/#A11005)) at 1:500 and anti-rabbit 647 (ThermoFisher/#A-21245) at 1:500 for 1 h at room temperature in the dark. Following washes, the sections were stained with DAPI (1 µg/mL, Sigma-Aldrich/Merck) for 10 min and then washed in PBS. The sections were mounted with PBS:Glycerol (1:1) before coverslipping.

A tandem mass tag (TMT) study employing a bottom-up liquid chromatography—tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) strategy was performed on 18 samples (ten IZ samples from
n

n

Tissue sample preparation and digestion
Tissue samples were homogenised in 6 M/2 M urea/thiourea, 10 mM DTT using a mechanical homogeniser. SDS was added to homogenate (2%) and bead beat for 1 x 20 sec at 4 degrees. Cellular debris was centrifuged out, and lysate left at room temperature for 30 min to allow for reduction. Lysates were alkylated with 55 mM IAA for 1 h (room temperature) in the dark. Proteins were precipitated with chloroform/MeOH and solubilised in 6 M/2 M urea/thiourea, 0.1 M HEPES, pH 8 and quantified using Qubit (Thermo Scientific [San Jose CA]). At this stage, protein aliquots from multiple samples were pooled to generate a “global standard” for internal normalisation of protein abundance. 50ug from each sample and the global standard were digested with trypsin (1:50) for 16 h at 37 degrees, 600 rpm using a ThermoMixer. Peptides were acidified to 1% (v/v) TFA and insoluble material removed by centrifugation at 12000 x
g
for 15 min. Peptides were desalted using hydrophilic-lipophilic balance (HLB) cartridges (Waters Corp., Milford MA) and dried by vacuum centrifugation.
Peptide labelling with Tandem Mass Tags (TMT)
20ug of peptides from each sample were labelled with TMTpro 16-plex (Thermo) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. Briefly, dried peptides were re-constituted in 0.1 M HEPES, pH 8.0 and quantified using qubit. TMT labels were re-constituted in 100% acetonitrile (MeCN) and added in equal volume to the peptide samples at a ratio of 1:2 (peptide:label). Labelling was performed for 2 h at room temperature, followed by quenching with 5% (v/v) hydroxylamine for 15 min. Samples were pooled 1:1 to generate two labelling experiments and dried by vacuum centrifugation. Labelled peptides were re-suspended in 0.1% TFA and purified to remove excess TMT label using HLB cartridges as described above, prior to drying by vacuum centrifugation.
Off-line MidpH fractionation
Dried peptides were re-suspended in 10 mM NH
4
HCO
2
, pH 7.9 and fractionated using midpH RP chromatography with a Waters XBridge BEH C
18
column (3.5 μm, 4.6 x 250 mm) on an Agilent 1260 HPLC using a 70 min gradient at a flow rate of 6 µL/min, resulting in a final 8 concatenated fractions.
Liquid Chromatography-Mass Spectrometry (LC-MS)/MS analysis
Labelled peptide fractions were re-constituted in 5% formic acid (FA) and analysed by LC-MS using an UltiMateTM 3000 HPLC System (Thermo Scientific) equipped with a C18 resin (1.9 μM) column for reversed phase separation that was coupled online to an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer (Thermo Scientific). Peptides were separated by increasing the concentration of the mobile phase over a 140 min gradient from 95% Buffer A (0.1% [v/v] formic acid), 5% Buffer B (80% [v/v] ACN, 0.1% [v/v] formic acid) to 95% Buffer B, 5% Buffer A at a flow rate of 300 nL min-1. Quantitation and peptide identification were carried out using a synchronous precursor selection (SPS)-based method. Briefly, MS1 and MS3 scans were acquired in the Orbitrap with a resolution of 120,000 and 60,000 respectively. The MS1 scan range was set to 400–1600
m/z
with a standard AGC target and dynamic exclusion set to 60 s. MS2 scans were acquired in the Iontrap with an intensity threshold of 5e3, standard AGC target, turbo scan rate, and an isolation window of 0.7
m/z
. Only precursors with charge state 2–6 were selected for MS2, and CID NCE was set to 35%. For reporter ion quantitation, 10 SPS precursors were selected for MS3 with HCD NCE of 55% within the mass range 100–500
m/z
, using a normalised AGC target of 500%. The duty cycle for the SP3-based method was set to 2.5 s.
LC-MS/MS data analysis
LC-MS/MS data were processed and analysed in Proteome Discoverer 2.5 (Thermo Scientific) and peptide spectral matches (PSMs) were searched using MASCOT
52
and Percolator
53
against a
Sus scrofa
translated genome database in FASTA format with the following parameters: precursor mass tolerance, 10 ppm; fragment mass tolerance, 0.2 Da; maximum missed trypsin cleavage sites, 2; dynamic modifications, methionine (Met) oxidation, cysteine (Cys) carbamidomethyl; and the quantitation method set to TMTpro 16plex. For reporter identification, a co-isolation threshold of 50%, average reporter S/N of 10, and SPS mass matches 65% was used, and protein abundances were normalised to control average (global standard, GS).
A matrix containing protein-identifications and their corresponding abundance intensities across multiple samples served as the primary dataset. Accompanying this matrix, a metadata file was used to associate sample IDs with key categorical information, including batch_names, zones, treatment or control categorizations, and condition details. Initially, proteins marked as contaminants by the protein identification tool were filtered out. Subsequently, a filter was applied to retain proteins supported by a minimum of 2 peptides for accurate identification. To ensure robustness, only proteins with abundance intensities identified across all samples within the cohort were retained for further analysis.
Median normalisation was performed using the normalize_sample_medians_df function from the R conductor proBatch package. Default parameters were applied for this process. Batch effects were corrected utilizing the correct_batch_effects_df function from proBatch ver. 1.8.0, also employing default parameters
54
.
To visualize relationships among samples, a set of custom functions were compiled within an R file named functions.R. These functions facilitated the generation of Principal Component Analysis (PCA) plots (qc_pca from protti), intensity distribution plots (qc_intensity_distribution from protti), and assessment of sample correlations (qc_sample_correlation from protti). This analysis served to confirm acceptable coefficient of variation values within conditions, typically falling below 15–20%.
Differential abundance analysis across pair-wise comparisons was conducted using the protti ver. 0.6.0 R package
55
. Gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) was performed to identify and visualise enriched Gene Ontology (GO) terms among differentially abundant proteins. Using the R package MSnID (version 3.18), protein identifiers were converted from RefSeq to Entrez Gene IDs using a species-specific conversion table and the fetch_conversion_table function. High confidence annotations were sourced from the Sus scrofa database org.Ss.eg.db. Functional enrichments of GO terms and WikiPathways was performed using clusterProfiler (version 4.9.4) gseGO and gseWP functions, respectively using default settings and leveraging ranked protein lists
56
. Enriched Reactome Pathways were identified using ReactomePA’s gsePathway function and organism set to “pig”. Proteins were ranked using a metric defined as −log10(p-value)×sign(diff). A minimum of 15 and a maximum of 500 genes per set were required for enrichment analyses. To refine GO terms, R package rrvgo’s (version 1.14.0-0) was run with default settings to reduce redundancy and cluster terms based on semantic similarity. Obsolete GO terms were excluded from further analysis.

The separation programme started with the isocratic elution with 1% mobile phase B at 0.4 mL/min (0–2 min) followed by an increase of mobile phase B to 55% at 0.4 mL/min (2–8 min) and reaching 99% of mobile phase B at 0.4 mL/min at 9 min. Thereafter, column was washed with 99% of mobile phase B at 0.6 mL/min (9–11 min), and equilibrated by returning to 1% of mobile phase B at 0.6 mL/min (11–14 min) and 1% of mobile phase B at 0.4 mL/min (15–20 min). Metabolites were analysed in positive and negative mode in MS
1

2

The electrospray settings were as follows: gas temperature 300 °C; drying gas flow 10 L/min; sheath gas temperature 300 °C; sheath gas flow 12 L/min; cap voltage: positive mode 3 kV, negative mode 3.5 kV. Blinding
Treatment allocation was randomized using a simple 1:1 computer generated randomization method. The operator performing the balloon inflations was blinded to treatment allocation until balloon deflation was performed. While we acknowledge that the presence of a mini-pump scar would provide identification of treatment allocation, all subsequent data collection and analysis was performed in a blinded fashion. To mitigate the knowledge of mini pump insertion, all animals had the anatomical location of the mini pump covered by a dressing at all times during the course of the study. Animals were only identified by a study ID until all data analysis was performed and unblinding to treatment allocation was allowed. MRI imaging was performed by an independent team that was blinded to treatment allocation. MRI scan analysis was performed on de-identified MRI study IDs. Invasive physiology data collection was performed in a blinded fashion and raw data was confirmed as accurate by an independent study researcher as per the prespecified protocol. Scar heterogeneity was performed with blinding to treatment allocation. Mult-omics analysis was performed by experts at an external collaborating institution who were blinded to treatment allocation. Vessel density analysis was performed on de-identified image series and researchers were blinded to treatment allocation as well as invasive physiology results. Electrophysiology team was blinded to treatment allocation at the time of performing the EPS as well as subsequent data analysis.
Statistical analysis
Sample size was calculated to detect a LVEF difference of 8.5 ± 2.5% between the two groups at day 28 post MI, based on the results from Thavapalachandran et al.
7
. To achieve 90% power and 0.05 significance (two-tailed), the necessary numbers were 4 animals per group. Statistical analyses were performed using IBM SPSS Statistics version 28 (IBM Corporation, New York, U.S.A). Continuous data are presented as mean ± SD or median (lower quartile, upper quartile) unless otherwise stated. Independent sample
t
-tests or Mann-Whitney
U
tests were performed (depending on data normality, as assessed by the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test). Independent samples median test used to compare the medians of LAVAs percentages across the 2 groups. Data for delta change from day 3 to day 30 and day 58 is presented as mean ± SD change from day 3 post infarct. This was tested for interaction with a repeated measures ANOVA first and only statistically significant parameters have been presented. Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA), followed by the Dunnett post hoc test to adjust for multiple comparisons, was performed for inter-group comparison of IMR and CFR.
P
values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant. For the proteomics analysis, log fold change ±1 with an adjusted
p
-value < 0.05 was considered significant. GSEA analysis was conducted using a ranking factor of [False Discovery Rate * Fold Change] with an adjusted
p
-value < 0.05 considered significant.
